description: We are Computer Science students from FEU Institute of Technology charting new frontiers in AI/ML, data engineering, data science, and software engineering. Our launchpad of skills includes Python, Java, JavaScript, React, databases, and web/mobile development. Join our crew to build mission-ready solutions, learn together, and launch bold ideas into orbit. We seek curious, collaborative co-pilots with skills in data analysis, UI/UX design, research, or storytelling.
summary:
CraterQuest is a browser-based strategy game for kids aged 7-12 that puts them in charge of a real lunar outpost near the Apollo 11 landing site. Trainees have to juggle Power, Warmth, and Food across 8 turns of Lunar Day and Night (each about 14 Earth days), manage a Radiation Badge with a 240 mSv mission budget, and earn Mission Stars by running science experiments.

Trainees can recruit 3 specialists: Engineer Kai, Botanist Mei, or Doctor Sol. Each bring unique abilities that affect gameplay on certain days, showing that space exploration is a team effort that combine strengths and perspectives against the greatest of challenges. 

Every number in the game is grounded in real NASA data: radiation doses come from NASA OCHMO career limits and Chang'E 4 surface measurements; solar storm doses from NASA NTRS; cold-night temperatures from LRO observations. Live solar particle storm dates are pulled from NASA's DONKI API, so the storm card shows a real event.

The game proves that every resource choice has a cause: a child who loses warmth learns exactly why (not enough heater cells at night), and the debrief traces each outcome back to the turn it was decided. A run-checker guarantees every seed is winnable before the player starts, and seed codes let players share and replay any run exactly1
details:
CraterQuest is a browser game that teaches real lunar survival trade-offs to children aged 7-12.

Players manage a Moon outpost in the Sea of Tranquility near the Apollo 11 landing site over eight turns of Lunar Day and Night (roughly 16 weeks). Each turn they split solar power across a Heater, a Greenhouse, an Experiments lab, and a storm Shelter, then answer an event card (dust storm, broken panels, science opportunities, etc.) that tests how well they planned. The outpost drawing reacts to their choices in real time: lights dim when power is low, frost appears when heat dies down, and the radiation badge ticks up with each turn.

The game covers all five challenge themes: life support (Food & Warmth bars), radiation shielding (the 12-pip Radiation Badge tied to NASA's 240 mSv career limit), power management (the daily solar-cell split), food (the Greenhouse system), and communications delay (cards modelled on the real ISS crew planning cycle). Real trade-offs are built into the rules: you cannot heat the habitat and run full experiments on the same turn unless you've saved spare cells. The debrief after each run links every outcome to the specific turn that caused it.

Most educational games tell kids facts. This game makes them feel the constraints real astronauts face. A child who loses the game because their radiation badge filled up learns that cosmic rays never stop. They also learn that burying the habitat under regolith actually helps. Every "real basis" note on a card cites a NASA source they can follow up.

The path to being an astronaut isn't always linear. What sets CraterQuest apart are 3 specialist characters (Engineer Kai, Botanist Mei, and Doctor Sol) that each unlock a third option on certain cards, so the same run plays differently depending on who you pick. By introducing them, we aim to inspire future astronauts by showing that exploration is a team effort where every skill matters. Every unexpected challenge can become opportunities to grow. A forecast one turn ahead gives players a chance to prepare for storms without making the game trivially easy. Stars can go negative, so there is always real cost to bad choices.

The game is built as a static web app — Vite + React + TypeScript for the menus, cards, bars and debrief screen, and Phaser 4 for the animated 2D outpost scene (sprite animations, lighting, particles and sound). The game engine is pure TypeScript with no React or Phaser imports, so the same rules run in the browser and in a Web Worker that checks every seed for winnability before play begins — the same guarantee, without blocking animations. Game state is managed with Zustand. A seeded random number generator (mulberry32) means the same seed code always replays the same run exactly. Seed codes include a typo-detecting checksum for safe sharing. DONKI space weather data is downloaded at build time and stored in the game, so every storm card references a real event with its date and source link; an optional “Today’s Sun” live mode makes one fresh DONKI call on game start and labels it LIVE, falling back to the archive labelled ARCHIVE if it fails. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages — free, HTTPS, and one stable URL for judges. All SI-assisted source files carry a disclosure header; AI_USAGE.md and si-manifest.json are in the repository root.

Here's how we used NASA Data!

  • NASA DONKI SEP API for mapping live solar particle storm dates to storm cards (falls back to sample data when offline).
  • NASARadLab API (ISS dosimetry) for the radiation science section in-game.
  • NASA OCHMO career radiation limits (600 mSv career, 240 mSv left for the commander). The basis of the Radiation Badge.
  • NASA NTRS references for solar storm dose estimates (~100 mSv on the lunar surface) and Apollo consumables planning.
  • Chang'E 4 cosmic-ray measurements (~1,369 µSv/day on the surface). The basis of the everyday radiation drip.
  • LRO surface temperature data. The basis of the -130°C night temperature and the Warmth rules.
